meta.framing: How do forensic investigators determine whether a corporate data breach was carried out by a malicious insider or by an external attacker using stolen credentials when the system logs initially support both explanations?

notes: The reference ladder. Only the conflict structure varies; atoms, topic and every other relation are held fixed, which is what makes the ordering attributable to coherence.

atoms.text: Meridian Financial detected the exfiltration of customer records from its database servers.
atoms.label: p1

atoms.text: The exfiltration sessions used the credentials of a senior database administrator.
atoms.label: p2

atoms.text: The suspicious logins occurred between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. local time.
atoms.label: p4

atoms.text: The administrator received a phishing email two weeks before the breach.
atoms.label: p5

atoms.text: The administrator's password was harvested through a phishing page.
atoms.label: p6

atoms.text: The administrator's session token was stolen from his home computer.
atoms.label: p7

atoms.text: Badge-access records showed the administrator was not in the building during the breach window.
atoms.label: p8

atoms.label: p9

atoms.label: p10

atoms.label: p14

atoms.text: The stolen customer records never appeared for sale anywhere.
atoms.label: p15
atoms.factual_note: exhaustive_pair: exactly one of this pair is false

response:
When system logs support both an insider and an external intrusion, forensic investigators stop treating the logs as a verdict. They treat them as one line of evidence to be checked against physical, behavioral and network records that an attacker cannot easily forge. The Meridian Financial case shows how the method works. Meridian Financial detected the exfiltration of customer records from its database servers; specifically, the exfiltrated data totaled 40 terabytes. A transfer of that scale fixed the scope of the incident and set the window that every later artifact had to be reconciled against.

The ambiguity began with authentication. The exfiltration sessions used the credentials of a senior database administrator. Investigators know that a valid credential shows only which account was used, not who was sitting at the keyboard. Authentication logs record that a secret was presented correctly. They cannot tell an owner acting deliberately from a stranger who has acquired the same secret. Investigators therefore rebuild the timeline of the account itself and look for the point at which control of it could have passed to someone else. The suspicious logins occurred between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. local time, and that activity came after the administrator received a phishing email two weeks before the breach. The email indicates that the administrator's password was harvested through a phishing page. Mail-gateway records and the landing page's own infrastructure tied the message to a credential-collection kit. The phishing route was not the only exposure, however. The password was harvested through that page. The administrator's session token was stolen from his home computer. Each path would let an outsider present the administrator's identity without his knowledge. A stolen session token would also explain how the attacker could bypass a password-only reset.

Physical-access data then narrowed the field. Whereas the overnight logins pointed to someone working inside the account in the small hours, badge-access records showed the administrator was not in the building during the breach window. Investigators weigh this kind of evidence heavily because it comes from a system separate from the network under examination. Endpoint analysis added a further complication: the administrator's corporate laptop had been encrypted by ransomware. Although the badge evidence placed him outside the premises, Meridian Financial's legal team argued that the administrator acted maliciously. In their view, absence from the building did not rule out remote action taken deliberately from elsewhere. By contrast with the ransomware damage to his laptop, the forensic firm's final report concluded that an external attacker carried out the breach using stolen credentials. That conclusion settled the dispute. The firm combined the phishing infrastructure, the token evidence and the access records into one account that the insider theory could not match.

Containment actions belong to the record as well, because they show when the defenders regained control. The administrator's account was disabled after the breach was discovered; in other words, following discovery of the breach, the company deactivated the administrator's login. Analysts track what happens downstream of such a step, since the attacker's response can reveal motive and affiliation. That deactivation led to the stolen customer records being later offered for sale on a dark-web marketplace. Threat-intelligence monitoring nonetheless left the question open in one direction only. Either the records were offered for sale in that way, or the stolen customer records never appeared for sale anywhere. The two cannot both be true, and one of them must hold. The FBI's cybercrime unit later determined that the records had in fact been listed on the dark-web marketplace, settling which alternative held.

The general lesson is that investigators settle an insider-versus-outsider question by triangulation, not by any single log. Credential use, the timing of compromise, physical presence, endpoint condition and the later movement of stolen data are each examined on their own terms. Only an explanation consistent with all of them is accepted as the finding.
